chunks.title: Identification and duty
chunks.text:
Fan F-401 is a direct-driven centrifugal fan with an 8-blade wheel, driven
by a 6-pole motor on a 60 Hz supply with no belt or gearbox between them.
Running speed is 1180 rpm, a shaft frequency of 19.7 Hz. The fan is assessed
for vibration under ISO 10816-3 group 2, flexible support, because it is
mounted on a spring-isolated base.

chunks.title: Wheel, shaft and bearing arrangement
chunks.text:
The wheel carries 8 blades and turns once per shaft revolution, so its
blade-pass frequency is 8 times shaft speed, 157 Hz. The shaft is carried
in an LDK UER204 insert bearing housed in a pillow block, with 8 rolling
elements. Its outer-race defect frequency (BPFO) is 3.083 times shaft
speed, 60.6 Hz.

chunks.title: Instrumentation
chunks.text:
One accelerometer is mounted radially on the bearing housing, reporting
acceleration in g. The duct instrumentation reports airflow, healthy at
about 4.0 m³/s, and a temperature sensor on the bearing housing reads a
healthy value of about 45 °C. These signals together carry the monitoring
evidence for this fan (see 5.7 and 5.8).

chunks.title: Lockout and tagout
chunks.text:
Before any work inside the fan casing or on the bearing, stop the fan,
isolate the drive motor at the local isolator, lock it and tag it with the
name of the person doing the work, and confirm the wheel has stopped
turning. The monitoring system is advisory only and must never be relied
on to keep the fan stopped.

chunks.title: Rotating wheel and guarding
chunks.text:
The coupling and shaft are guarded at the drive end; never reach past a
guard while the fan is running. Keep hands, tools and loose clothing clear
of the inlet and outlet openings, since the wheel continues to turn under
its own inertia for some time after the motor is switched off.

chunks.title: Entry into the fan housing
chunks.text:
Before anyone enters the fan housing, isolate and lock out the drive (see
2.1), close and lock any dampers that could admit a flow of air, and
confirm the wheel is fully stopped by direct observation through the
inspection door, not from the control room reading alone.

chunks.title: Airflow and pressure
chunks.text:
Airflow is measured by a duct sensor downstream of the fan outlet and
trended against the 4.0 m³/s baseline at the normal system resistance. A
falling reading at unchanged fan speed points first to the fan itself (see
5.4) rather than to the sensor, once damper and filter position are ruled
out (see 3.2).

chunks.title: Dampers and filters
chunks.text:
Confirm damper position and filter condition before treating a low-airflow
reading as a fan fault: a partly closed damper or a loaded filter raises
system resistance and lowers flow with the fan itself unchanged. Airflow
readings are only compared against the baseline with dampers and filters
in their normal running condition.

chunks.title: Bearing temperature
chunks.text:
The bearing housing temperature sensor is read continuously and trended
against the 45 °C baseline. A rise with steady vibration points to a
lubrication or cooling problem; a rise together with rising vibration and
BPFO impacts points to a developing bearing fault (see 5.6).

chunks.title: Wheel cleaning
chunks.text:
Dirt and process residue build up unevenly on the wheel blades and shift
the wheel's mass distribution, producing unbalance (see 5.3). Wheel
cleaning is done with the fan isolated (see 2.1), by hand or with a
low-pressure wash as the process allows, working blade by blade rather than
spraying across the whole wheel at once.

chunks.title: Wheel inspection and blade repair
chunks.text:
Inspect every blade for a cracked blade, a bent or eroded leading edge, and
a fouled blade carrying residue that cleaning has not removed. A cracked
blade is not repaired in place; replace the wheel. Minor erosion is
recorded and trended, and a fouled blade is scheduled for wheel cleaning
(see 4.1) rather than repair.

chunks.title: Balancing
chunks.text:
Where unbalance is confirmed by vibration evidence (see 5.3) and wheel
cleaning has not resolved it, trim-balance the wheel in place with weights
fitted to the balancing rim. Balance to the grade specified for this fan
class. Unbalance that returns quickly after balancing points to ongoing
fouling or erosion rather than a one-off imbalance.

chunks.title: Bearing lubrication and replacement
chunks.text:
Regrease the pillow block bearing on the interval set for its duty and
ambient temperature, using the grease grade specified for the LDK UER204.
To replace the bearing, isolate the fan (see 2.1), support the shaft,
withdraw the worn insert from its housing, fit the replacement to the
shaft, and lock its collar before removing the shaft support.

chunks.title: Mounting and base bolts
chunks.text:
Check all base and pillow-block hold-down bolts for tightness at scheduled
inspection; a loose base or a hold-down bolt backed off produces mechanical
looseness in the vibration signature (see 5.5). Retorque to the specified
value and inspect the isolation springs for damage or uneven compression.

chunks.title: Inlet cone clearance
chunks.text:
Check the running clearance between the wheel inlet and the inlet cone
against the drawing value at scheduled inspection. A clearance that has
closed up indicates shaft or bearing wear and is investigated with the
vibration evidence before the clearance is reset.

chunks.title: Vibration severity zones
chunks.text:
Overall vibration is assessed as velocity RMS over 10–1000 Hz against
ISO 10816-3 group 2, flexible support: zone A below 2.3 mm/s, zone B to
4.5 mm/s, zone C to 7.1 mm/s, zone D above. The bearing-housing
accelerometer signal is integrated to velocity for this assessment.

chunks.title: Blade-pass frequency
chunks.text:
Blade-pass frequency is the blade count times shaft speed: 8 times 19.7 Hz,
157 Hz at nominal speed. Its amplitude reflects how evenly the wheel
delivers flow to the volute and is the reference feature against which
sidebands from blade damage are measured (see 5.4).

chunks.title: Unbalance
chunks.text:
Unbalance from dirt build-up or erosion on the wheel raises the vibration
at shaft speed, 1X, with little immediate change in airflow or bearing
temperature. It is the most common fault on this fan class. Confirm with
wheel cleaning (see 4.1) before resorting to balancing (see 4.3).

chunks.title: Blade damage and fouling
chunks.text:
Blade damage — a cracked blade, a bent or eroded blade, or a fouled blade —
produces sidebands at blade-pass frequency plus and minus shaft speed, a
modest rise in the blade-pass amplitude itself, and a reduction in airflow.
Confirm with a wheel inspection (see 4.2) before the fan is returned to
service.

chunks.title: Mechanical looseness
chunks.text:
Mechanical looseness, from a loose base, a backed-off hold-down bolt or a
deteriorated foundation, raises vibration at twice and three times shaft
speed and introduces a half-order subharmonic component not present in a
healthy spectrum. Correct by retorquing the mounting and base bolts (see
4.5) and inspecting the isolation springs.

chunks.title: Bearing outer-race wear
chunks.text:
Outer-race wear of the pillow-block bearing produces impacts at BPFO,
60.6 Hz at nominal speed, visible in the envelope spectrum together with a
rise in kurtosis, and the bearing runs hot. Advanced outer-race spalling
raises the plain-spectrum level as well. Plan the bearing replacement (see
4.4) once envelope impacts are confirmed.

chunks.title: Airflow trend
chunks.text:
Airflow is trended against the 4.0 m³/s baseline once damper and filter
position are confirmed normal (see 3.2). A falling trend with rising
blade-pass sidebands supports blade damage (see 5.4); a falling trend with
no vibration evidence points back to the duct system rather than the fan.

chunks.title: Bearing temperature trend
chunks.text:
Bearing temperature is trended against the 45 °C baseline. A rise with
steady vibration points to lubrication; a rise together with rising BPFO
impacts and rising kurtosis supports bearing outer-race wear (see 5.6)
rather than a lubrication problem alone.

chunks.title: Alarm response
chunks.text:
On any WATCH or WARNING, confirm the reading first: check that the
accelerometer is secure, that the fan is at steady load, and that the
supply is normal. Then follow the section for the fault the evidence points
to. A CRITICAL state is an advisory to plan a stop under lockout (see 2.1);
the plant protection system remains in charge of stopping the fan.

chunks.title: Start-up
chunks.text:
Confirm dampers are in their start position and the wheel turns freely by
hand before starting after an extended shutdown (see 2.1 for isolation
during the check). Bring the fan up to speed and allow airflow to settle
before comparing the reading to baseline; readings during the first minute
are excluded from alarms.

chunks.title: Shutdown
chunks.text:
Open dampers to their running position before stopping where the process
allows, to avoid a sudden pressure change across the wheel. After a stop of
more than a week, turn the wheel by hand before restarting to confirm it
turns freely and redistribute bearing grease across the insert.

chunks.title: What to record
chunks.text:
Record every wheel cleaning, blade inspection, balancing job, bearing
replacement and mounting check against the fan and the date, together with
the airflow and vibration baseline taken after each intervention. The
baseline after maintenance is what later alarms are judged against.

chunks.title: Identification and duty
chunks.text:
Gearbox GB-201 is a single-stage parallel-shaft reducer rated at 30 kW. A
37-tooth helical pinion on the input shaft drives a 74-tooth wheel, a 2:1
reduction. The input runs at a nominal 1480 rpm, a running frequency of
24.7 Hz, so the output turns at 740 rpm. The gear mesh frequency — teeth times
input shaft frequency — is 912.7 Hz. The gearbox is assessed under ISO 10816-3
group 2 on a rigid foundation.

chunks.title: Gear and bearing arrangement
chunks.text:
The input shaft runs in a 6207 deep-groove ball bearing at the drive end, with
nine rolling elements of 11.1 mm on a 46.0 mm pitch circle and a contact angle
of zero. At 1480 rpm its outer-race defect frequency (BPFO) is 84.2 Hz and its
cage frequency is 9.4 Hz, 0.379 times shaft speed. These figures set the
monitoring configuration and must be re-entered if a different bearing is
fitted, as must the tooth count if the gear set is changed (see 5.2).

chunks.title: Instrumentation
chunks.text:
One accelerometer is mounted radially on the input bearing housing, reporting
acceleration in g, and a resistance thermometer sits in the oil sump. The
monitoring system derives from the accelerometer the overall level, the shaft
harmonics, the gear mesh frequency, its second harmonic and its sidebands, the
bearing defect frequency and the cage frequency in the envelope spectrum.

chunks.title: Lockout and tagout
chunks.text:
Before any work inside the guard or on the gearbox, stop the drive, isolate
the motor at the local isolator, lock it and tag it with the name of the person
doing the work, and prove zero energy by attempting a start. The monitoring
system is advisory only: it never stops the gearbox and must never be relied on
to keep it stopped.

chunks.title: Hot oil and rotating parts
chunks.text:
Sump oil can exceed 70 °C in service. Allow the gearbox to cool before opening
inspection covers or draining oil, and wear gloves and eye protection. Keep
hands, tools and loose clothing clear of the couplings while the drive is
running; inspections of rotating parts are done by stroboscope, not by touch.

chunks.title: Lifting
chunks.text:
The gearbox weighs 310 kg with oil. Lift only by the two cast lifting eyes on
the upper casing, never by the shafts, and drain the oil first when the
gearbox is to be removed from its base.

chunks.title: Oil and oil changes
chunks.text:
The gearbox is splash-lubricated with an ISO VG 220 mineral gear oil to the
level mark on the sight glass. Change the oil every 4000 running hours or
yearly, whichever comes first, and after the first 500 hours of a new gear
set. Never mix oils of different grades or base stocks.

chunks.title: Oil analysis
chunks.text:
Take an oil sample from the drain valve with the gearbox warm, every 1000
hours and whenever an alarm is raised. Rising iron particle counts indicate
wear of the gear teeth or the bearing; a sudden rise in large particles after a
period of steady readings indicates a tooth or bearing surface breaking up.

chunks.title: Oil temperature
chunks.text:
The sump runs at about 55 °C at nominal load. A sustained rise of 10 °C above
the regime baseline indicates increased friction — wear of the gear teeth, a
failing bearing, misalignment or low oil level — and is investigated with the
vibration evidence. Do not run the gearbox above 85 °C sump temperature.

chunks.title: Gear mesh inspection
chunks.text:
With the drive isolated (see 2.1), remove the inspection cover and turn the
input by hand. Check every pinion tooth for pitting, scuffing, spalling and
cracks at the root. Apply marking compound to three wheel teeth and turn the
set through mesh to record the contact pattern; a pattern concentrated at one
end of the face indicates misalignment (see 4.4).

chunks.title: Gear set replacement
chunks.text:
Replace the pinion and the wheel together; a new pinion run against a worn
wheel wears out quickly. Drain the oil, remove the upper casing, withdraw both
shafts, and press the gears off with a hydraulic puller. Fit new gears at the
interference stated on the drawing, reassemble, set the backlash (see 4.6), and
refill with fresh oil (see 3.1).

chunks.title: Input bearing replacement
chunks.text:
With the oil drained, remove the input bearing cover and withdraw the shaft.
Pull the bearing with a puller acting on the inner ring only, heat the new
bearing by induction to 110 °C, and slide it on against the shoulder. Never
drive a bearing on with a hammer. Record the fitting date against the bearing
position.

chunks.title: Shaft alignment
chunks.text:
Misalignment between the motor and the input shaft loads the input bearing and
the gear teeth unevenly. Align with a laser system to within 0.05 mm offset and
0.05 mm per 100 mm angularity, with the gearbox at operating temperature or with
the thermal growth allowed for. Check for soft foot under every hold-down
before aligning.

chunks.title: Coupling inspection
Backlash check
chunks.text:
Measure backlash with a dial indicator on a wheel tooth while holding the
pinion. The specified range is 0.15–0.25 mm. Backlash above 0.35 mm indicates
tooth wear and is a reason to plan gear set replacement (see 4.2).

chunks.title: Vibration severity zones
chunks.text:
Overall vibration is assessed as velocity RMS over 10–1000 Hz against ISO
10816-3 group 2, rigid foundation: zone A below 1.4 mm/s, zone B to 2.8 mm/s,
zone C to 4.5 mm/s, zone D above. The accelerometer signal is integrated to
velocity for this. The gear mesh at 912.7 Hz lies near the top of the band, so
gear faults show earlier in the mesh features than in the overall level.

chunks.title: Gear mesh frequency
chunks.text:
The gear mesh frequency is the tooth count times the shaft frequency: 37 times
24.7 Hz, 912.7 Hz at nominal speed. Its amplitude and that of its second
harmonic at 1825 Hz reflect how smoothly the teeth transfer load. Both rise as
the tooth profiles wear, and the second harmonic rises faster, because wear
distorts the profile from the involute shape.

chunks.title: Sidebands
chunks.text:
A gear that is not uniform around its circumference modulates the mesh once per
revolution, and the modulation appears as sidebands at the mesh frequency plus
and minus the shaft frequency. Low sidebands are normal. Sidebands that grow
quickly, or come to match the mesh amplitude, indicate damage localised on one
tooth or eccentricity of the gear.

chunks.title: Tooth wear
chunks.text:
Distributed wear of the tooth flanks raises the gear mesh amplitude and, more
strongly, its second harmonic, with a modest rise in sidebands and a rise in
oil temperature. Confirm with oil analysis (see 3.2) and backlash (see 4.6).
Wear that is still in its early stage is managed by oil change and monitoring;
advanced wear calls for gear set replacement (see 4.2).

chunks.title: Broken or cracked tooth
chunks.text:
A cracked or broken tooth strikes once per revolution of its shaft as it enters
mesh. The signal becomes impulsive: kurtosis, crest factor and peak rise, and
the mesh sidebands grow strongly while the mesh amplitude itself may change
little. Stop the gearbox at the next opportunity and inspect the teeth (see
4.1); running on risks the fragment damaging the other gear and the bearings.

chunks.title: Misalignment
chunks.text:
Misalignment of the input shaft raises the amplitude at shaft speed and
especially at twice shaft speed, with a moderate rise in oil temperature. The
gear contact pattern moves to one end of the face (see 4.1). Correct with a
soft-foot check, coupling inspection and laser alignment (see 4.4 and 4.5).

chunks.title: Input bearing outer-race wear
chunks.text:
Outer-race spalling of the input bearing produces impacts at BPFO, 84.2 Hz at
nominal speed, visible in the envelope spectrum rather than the plain spectrum,
and often modulated at the cage frequency. Kurtosis rises and the oil warms.
Confirm by listening and by oil analysis, then plan the bearing replacement
(see 4.3); a spalled race progresses faster once the oil carries its debris.

chunks.title: Oil temperature trend
chunks.text:
Oil temperature is trended against the baseline of the same duty regime. A
rise with no vibration evidence points first to the oil level and the oil
itself (see 3.1); a rise together with vibration evidence supports the fault
that evidence names (see 5.4 to 5.7).

chunks.title: Alarm response
chunks.text:
On any WATCH or WARNING, confirm the reading before acting: check that the
sensor is secure, that the regime is steady, and that the oil level is
correct. Then follow the section for the fault the evidence points to. A
CRITICAL state is an advisory to plan a stop under lockout (see 2.1); the plant
protection system remains in charge of stopping the drive.

chunks.title: Start-up
chunks.text:
Check the oil level on the sight glass before every start. Start unloaded
where the process allows and bring the load up over five minutes; a cold oil
film carries load poorly. Readings during the first minutes after a start are
excluded from alarms.

chunks.title: Shutdown
chunks.text:
Remove the load before stopping the drive. After a long stop, turn the input
by hand before restarting to redistribute the oil over the teeth.

chunks.title: What to record
chunks.text:
Record every oil change, oil sample result, backlash reading, alignment and
component replacement against the gearbox and the date, with the vibration
baseline taken after each intervention. The baseline after maintenance is what
later alarms are judged against.

chunks.title: Responding to an unrecognised change
chunks.text:
This is Harmonic's own general guidance, not this machine's manual: no
manual is on file for this machine or its family.

Confirm the reading with a second measurement at the same duty point before
acting on it. Inspect the machine manually — listen, look and feel for the
obvious, such as leaks, loose guards, unusual heat or unusual noise — before
opening anything up.

Before any mechanical work, lock out and tag out the machine's own isolation
point and verify zero energy; this advisory never substitutes for that step.

The plant's own operating and maintenance procedures for this machine take
precedence over this guidance wherever the two differ.

chunks.title: Identification and duty
chunks.text:
Motor M-301 is a 4-pole three-phase induction motor rated 2.2 kW on a 60 Hz
supply. Synchronous speed is 1800 rpm; at full load the rotor runs at
1710 rpm, a slip of 5%, giving a shaft frequency of 28.5 Hz. The motor drives
its load through a direct coupling and is assessed for vibration under
ISO 10816-1 class I.

chunks.title: Rotor, stator and bearing arrangement
chunks.text:
The squirrel-cage rotor turns in an SKF 6205-2RS JEM deep groove ball
bearing at the drive end, with nine rolling elements. At 1710 rpm its
outer-race defect frequency (BPFO) is 3.585 times shaft speed, 102.2 Hz, and
its cage frequency is 0.398 times shaft speed. The non-drive end carries a
matching sealed bearing that is not separately monitored.

chunks.title: Instrumentation
chunks.text:
One accelerometer is mounted radially at the drive-end bearing housing,
reporting acceleration in g. A resistance temperature detector embedded in
the stator winding reads a healthy value of about 72 °C at rated load, and
the supply feeder reports phase current, healthy at about 8.2 A. These three
signals together carry the monitoring evidence for this motor (see 5.8).

chunks.title: Lockout and electrical isolation
chunks.text:
Before any work on the motor or its terminal box, open and lock the local
isolator, tag it with the name of the person doing the work, and prove the
terminals dead with a voltage tester before touching them. The monitoring
system is advisory only: it never removes power from the motor and must
never be relied on to keep it isolated.

chunks.title: Rotating parts and hot surfaces
chunks.text:
The coupling and shaft extension are guarded; never reach past a guard while
the motor is running. The frame and the drive-end bearing housing can reach
80 °C in normal service, hotter under a developing fault, so allow the motor
to cool before touching it and rely on the temperature reading rather than
touch for a check.

chunks.title: Lifting
chunks.text:
The motor weighs 32 kg. Lift by the frame eyebolt only, never by the
terminal box or the shaft, and support the load with a sling rated for the
full weight before disconnecting the mounting bolts.

chunks.title: Supply and protection
chunks.text:
The motor is fed through a thermal-magnetic breaker and a contactor sized
for its full-load current. Confirm the supply voltage is balanced across the
three phases within 2% before starting; a sustained unbalance loads one
phase winding more than the others and behaves, electrically and thermally,
like a stator winding fault (see 5.5).

chunks.title: Insulation resistance test
chunks.text:
With the motor isolated (see 2.1) and the terminals disconnected from the
supply, measure insulation resistance from each phase winding to frame with
a 500 V insulation tester. A reading below 1 MΩ, or one that has fallen
sharply since the last test, indicates moisture or winding degradation and
the motor should not be re-energised until the cause is found.

chunks.title: Winding temperature
chunks.text:
The embedded RTD is read continuously and trended against the 72 °C
baseline at rated load. A rise with steady current and steady vibration
points to a cooling-path problem such as a blocked fan or fouled fins; a
rise together with a rising current points to an electrical cause (see 5.5
and 5.8).

chunks.title: Bearing lubrication
chunks.text:
The drive-end bearing is sealed (2RS) and is not designed to be regreased in
service; do not attempt to add grease through the shield. Check instead for
grease discolouration and bearing temperature at scheduled inspections, and
plan replacement (see 4.2) once the sealed charge is judged exhausted rather
than topping it up.

chunks.title: Drive-end bearing replacement
chunks.text:
With the motor isolated and the rotor withdrawn, pull the bearing from the
shaft with a puller acting on the inner ring, never through the balls. Heat
the replacement SKF 6205-2RS JEM by induction to about 100 °C before
fitting, seat it against the shaft shoulder, and record the fitting date
against the drive-end position.

chunks.title: Rotor inspection and bar testing
chunks.text:
Where broken rotor bar evidence is present (see 5.4), an offline growler or
current-injection bar test locates the affected bars directly. Inspect
visible end-ring joints for cracking or discolouration from overheating. A
rotor with more than one confirmed broken bar is not economic to repair and
is normally replaced as an assembly.

chunks.title: Balancing
chunks.text:
Residual rotor unbalance, or unbalance introduced by a coupling half or a
fan, is corrected by trim-balancing at the coupling end with the motor
running free. Balance to the grade specified on the nameplate. Repeated
unbalance after balancing points to a bent shaft or a loose rotor core and
is not solved by adding further trim weight.

chunks.title: Alignment and soft foot
chunks.text:
Check for soft foot at each of the four feet, one bolt loosened at a time,
before aligning the motor to its load; a foot that moves more than 0.05 mm
must be shimmed flat before alignment proceeds. Align with a laser system to
within 0.05 mm offset and 0.05 mm per 100 mm angularity.

chunks.title: Stator winding repair
chunks.text:
A confirmed stator winding fault, such as shorted turns found by the
insulation resistance test (see 3.2) or a growing surge-test difference
between phases, is not field-repairable on this frame size. Isolate the
motor, tag it out of service, and rewind or replace it; running on
risks a phase-to-phase or phase-to-earth failure.

chunks.title: Vibration severity zones
chunks.text:
Overall vibration is assessed as velocity RMS over 10–1000 Hz against
ISO 10816-1 class I: zone A below 0.71 mm/s, zone B to 1.8 mm/s, zone C to
4.5 mm/s, zone D above. The drive-end accelerometer signal is integrated to
velocity for this assessment.

chunks.title: Running speed and slip
chunks.text:
Shaft frequency at full load is 28.5 Hz, against a synchronous 30 Hz, a
slip of 5%. Slip rises with load and falls as the motor lightens, so the
running-speed peak in the spectrum is expected to drift slightly with duty
and is not itself a fault indication.

chunks.title: Twice line frequency
chunks.text:
A component at twice the line frequency, 120 Hz, order 4.21 relative to
shaft speed, is normally low and steady. A rise in this component, taken
together with rising winding temperature and rising current, is the primary
vibration signature of an electrical fault in the stator (see 5.5) rather
than a mechanical one.

chunks.title: Broken rotor bars
chunks.text:
A broken rotor bar, or broken rotor bars, unbalance the rotor's magnetic
field once per slip cycle, producing sidebands at shaft frequency plus and
minus the pole-pass frequency, four times the slip frequency, 6 Hz at full
load. The same fault shows as a slow swing in phase current at the 6 Hz
pole-pass rate. Confirm with a bar test (see 4.3).

chunks.title: Stator winding faults
chunks.text:
Shorted turns or a developing stator winding fault raise the 120 Hz
vibration component, raise the winding temperature reading, and raise
phase current, together rather than singly. Supply voltage unbalance
produces the same three-part signature and should be ruled out first (see
3.1) before opening the motor for a winding fault.

chunks.title: Unbalance
chunks.text:
Mechanical unbalance of the rotor or a coupled component raises the
vibration at shaft speed, 1X, with little change in current or temperature.
It is the most common mechanical fault on this motor class and is corrected
by trim-balancing (see 4.4) once other 1X causes, such as a bent shaft, are
ruled out.

chunks.title: Drive-end bearing outer-race wear
chunks.text:
Outer-race wear of the drive-end bearing produces impacts at BPFO, 102.2 Hz
at full-load speed, visible in the envelope spectrum together with a rise
in kurtosis. Advanced outer-race spalling raises the plain-spectrum
overall level as well. Plan the bearing replacement (see 4.2) once envelope
impacts are confirmed and trending upward.

chunks.title: Current and temperature trends
chunks.text:
Phase current and winding temperature are trended against their 8.2 A and
72 °C baselines at rated load. Both rising together points to an electrical
cause (see 5.5); temperature rising alone points to cooling; current alone
swinging at the pole-pass rate points to broken rotor bars (see 5.4).

chunks.title: Alarm response
chunks.text:
On any WATCH or WARNING, confirm the reading first: check that the
accelerometer is secure, that the load is steady, and that the supply is
normal. Then follow the section for the fault the evidence points to. A
CRITICAL state is an advisory to plan a stop under lockout (see 2.1); the
plant protection system remains in charge of stopping the motor.

chunks.title: Starting
chunks.text:
Confirm the supply is balanced (see 3.1) and the insulation resistance test
is current (see 3.2) before starting after an extended shutdown. Bring the
motor up to speed unloaded where the process allows, and exclude readings
taken during the first minute of running from alarm evaluation while
starting current settles.

chunks.title: Stopping
chunks.text:
Remove the driven load before stopping where the process allows. After a
stop of more than a week, bar the rotor over by hand before restarting to
confirm it turns freely and to redistribute bearing grease across the
raceway.

chunks.title: What to record
chunks.text:
Record every insulation resistance test, bearing replacement, balancing
job, alignment check and winding repair against the motor and the date,
together with the vibration and current baseline taken after each
intervention. The baseline after maintenance is what later alarms are
judged against.

chunks.title: Identification and duty
chunks.text:
Pump P-101 is a horizontal end-suction centrifugal pump driven by a 45 kW
four-pole induction motor through a flexible jaw coupling. Nominal shaft speed
is 2950 rpm, which places the running frequency at 49.2 Hz. Rated duty is
120 m³/h against 4.2 bar discharge at 0.65 load factor. The pump is classed as
a machine under ISO 10816-1 class III, rigid foundation. All vibration
limits quoted in this manual are velocity RMS in mm/s measured radially at the
bearing housings over the 10–1000 Hz band.

chunks.title: Bearing arrangement
chunks.text:
Both ends carry deep-groove ball bearings with nine rolling elements, a ball
diameter of 7.94 mm and a pitch diameter of 38.5 mm, mounted at a nominal
contact angle of zero degrees. The drive-end bearing takes the radial load from
the impeller; the non-drive end is the locating bearing and takes axial thrust.
These geometry figures are what set the defect frequencies in section 5.2, and
they must be re-entered in the monitoring configuration whenever a bearing of a
different type is fitted.

chunks.title: Instrumentation
chunks.text:
The machine carries a radial accelerometer at each bearing housing sampled at
25.6 kHz, an axial accelerometer at the drive end, RTDs in both bearing
housings and in the motor winding, pressure transmitters on the suction and
discharge flanges, a magnetic flow meter on the discharge line, and a motor
current transducer. The slow channels are sampled once per second. Vibration is
integrated to velocity in the acquisition chain, so all amplitudes in this
manual are velocity unless a section says otherwise.

chunks.title: Operating regimes
chunks.text:
The pump runs in four steady regimes and one transient. `IDLE` is below 500 rpm.
`STARTUP` is any period where shaft speed is changing by more than 100 rpm per
second, regardless of the speed reached. `NOMINAL` is 2800–3000 rpm at a load
factor between 0.5 and 0.8. `HIGH_LOAD` is the same speed band above 0.8 load.
`LOW_LOAD` is the same speed band below 0.5 load, which is the regime most
associated with recirculation and cavitation. Baselines are held separately per
regime because the same vibration level means different things in each.

chunks.title: Lockout and tagout
chunks.text:
Isolate the motor at the local disconnect, apply a personal lock and tag, and
verify zero energy at the motor terminals before any mechanical work. The
locking-out step is not optional for inspection work: a pump on automatic level
control can start without warning. Prove the isolation by attempting a local
start after the lock is applied.

chunks.title: Pressure and fluid hazards
chunks.text:
Close and lock the suction and discharge isolation valves, then vent the casing
through the high-point vent before breaking any flanged joint. The casing can
hold pressure after the valves are shut. Where the pumped fluid is hot, allow
the casing to cool below 40 °C before draining, and drain to a closed system
where the fluid is hazardous.

chunks.title: Hot surfaces and rotating parts
chunks.text:
Bearing housings can exceed 80 °C in normal running and the motor frame can
exceed 70 °C. Never remove the coupling guard while the machine is energised.
The guard is also the alignment access cover, so alignment work always follows
the lockout in section 2.1.

chunks.title: Lifting
chunks.text:
The bare pump weighs 310 kg and the motor 295 kg. Lift the pump by the casing
lugs, never by the suction nozzle or the coupling. Support the rotor during
bearing work so the shaft does not sit on the seal faces.

chunks.title: Lubrication schedule
chunks.text:
Both bearings are grease-lubricated with a lithium-complex NLGI 2 grease.
Regrease every 2000 running hours with 18 g per bearing at the drive end and
14 g at the non-drive end. Purge the old grease through the relief port with
the machine running at nominal speed; regreasing a stationary bearing packs the
cavity and raises the running temperature. Record every regrease against the
running-hour counter, because the interval is the commonest thing to lose track
of after a shutdown.

chunks.title: Grease compatibility
chunks.text:
Do not mix lithium-complex grease with polyurea or calcium-sulphonate grease.
Mixed thickeners soften, the base oil bleeds out and the bearing runs dry with
no visible change in the fill level. If the grease in service is unknown, flush
the cavity completely as in section 3.4 rather than topping up.

chunks.title: Over-greasing
chunks.text:
An over-greased bearing churns, and the churning shows as a rising bearing
temperature with little change in vibration — typically 10 to 20 °C above the
regime baseline within an hour of the regrease. Relieve the excess by running
with the relief port open for thirty minutes. Persistent over-greasing damages
the cage and eventually produces the wear pattern in section 5.4.

chunks.title: Grease flush procedure
chunks.text:
Isolate per section 2.1. Remove the relief plug and the fill plug, inject fresh
grease at the fill port until clean grease emerges at the relief port, refit
both plugs, and run at nominal for thirty minutes with the relief port open.
Allow two hours for the bearing temperature to settle before comparing it
against the baseline. Budget 45 minutes per bearing.

chunks.title: Lubricant contamination
chunks.text:
Water or process fluid in the grease destroys the load-carrying film and
produces outer-race damage within a few hundred running hours. Suspect
contamination when the bearing temperature rises alongside broadband vibration
and the machine has recently run with a leaking seal. Contaminated grease is a
cause of outer-race wear, not a symptom of it, and replacing the bearing
without curing the ingress path repeats the failure.

chunks.title: Bearing inspection
chunks.text:
Inspect the bearings whenever the overall vibration at a bearing housing
exceeds 4.5 mm/s RMS, when the bearing temperature runs more than 15 °C above
the regime baseline, or at 16000 running hours, whichever comes first. Listen
with a stethoscope at the housing: a regular tick at shaft speed indicates a
local defect, while a rough continuous hiss indicates general wear or
contamination.

chunks.title: Bearing replacement procedure
chunks.text:
Isolate per section 2.1 and drain per section 2.2. Remove the coupling guard,
mark the coupling halves for reassembly and withdraw the coupling with a
two-leg puller. Remove the bearing end cover, release the locknut and tab
washer, and withdraw the bearing with a bearing puller applied to the inner
ring only. Never drive the replacement bearing on through the outer ring:
induction-heat the new bearing to 110 °C and slide it onto the shaft, then hold
it against the shoulder until it grips. Refit the tab washer and locknut, pack
the housing to one third with the grease in section 3.1, refit the end cover,
and refit the coupling to the marks. Realign per section 4.4 before removing
the lockout. Allow three hours, technician level, with a bearing puller and an
induction heater.

chunks.title: Bearing fitting tolerances
chunks.text:
The shaft seat is 45 mm k5 and the housing bore is 85 mm H6. Check both before
fitting: a worn shaft seat lets the inner ring creep, which produces a
fretting pattern and a vibration signature that returns within weeks of a
bearing change. A housing bore above tolerance allows the outer ring to turn
and polishes the bore. Neither fault is cured by fitting another bearing.

chunks.title: Shaft alignment
chunks.text:
Align cold with a laser alignment system, targeting 0.05 mm parallel offset and
0.05 mm per 100 mm angular at the coupling. Shim under all four motor feet and
check for soft foot before correcting the alignment: a soft foot makes the
readings change as the hold-down bolts are tightened, and correcting alignment
onto a soft foot builds the error into the machine. Recheck hot after two hours
at nominal duty and record both sets of readings. Allow two hours, technician
level.

chunks.title: Coupling inspection
chunks.text:
Inspect the jaw coupling elastomer at every alignment. A hardened, cracked or
powdered element transmits misalignment forces straight into both bearings and
raises the 2X vibration component without any change in the alignment readings
themselves. Replace the element in pairs and never mix durometer grades.

chunks.title: Mechanical seal replacement
chunks.text:
Isolate and drain per section 2. Remove the seal gland bolts, withdraw the
gland and the rotating assembly, and inspect the shaft sleeve for scoring.
Fit the new seal dry-handed, with the faces protected until the last moment.
Set the working length from the sleeve shoulder to the dimension on the seal
drawing. Pressure-test to 1.5 times working pressure before returning to
service. Allow two hours, technician level.

chunks.title: Impeller inspection
chunks.text:
Withdraw the casing cover and inspect the impeller vanes for pitting on the
low-pressure side of the leading edge, which is the signature of cavitation
damage rather than of erosion by solids. Measure the wear-ring clearance: the
design clearance is 0.35 mm diametral and the replacement limit is 0.70 mm.
Worn wear rings raise internal recirculation, which lowers delivered flow at
constant speed and mimics a seal leak on the flow channel alone.

chunks.title: Foundation and hold-down
chunks.text:
Check the grout for cracking and the hold-down bolts for torque annually.
A loose hold-down produces a vibration signature at 2X and 3X shaft speed with
a strongly directional character, which is easily confused with misalignment
and is distinguished by the fact that alignment readings are within tolerance.

chunks.title: Vibration severity zones
chunks.text:
ISO 10816-1 class III sets four zones by velocity RMS over 10–1000 Hz. Zone A,
below 1.8 mm/s, is a newly commissioned machine. Zone B, 1.8 to 4.5 mm/s, is
acceptable for unrestricted long-term operation. Zone C, 4.5 to 11.2 mm/s, is
unsatisfactory for continuous operation and the machine should be scheduled for
correction. Zone D, above 11.2 mm/s, is severe enough to cause damage and the
machine should be stopped. A machine of 28 mm/s or more is in immediate danger.
These are absolute limits; a rise within a zone is still significant if it is a
rise against that machine's own baseline.

chunks.title: Bearing defect frequencies
chunks.text:
For the bearing in section 1.2 at 2950 rpm, the ball-pass frequency of the
outer race (BPFO) is 151.3 Hz, the ball-pass frequency of the inner race (BPFI)
is 291.2 Hz, and the ball-spin frequency (BSF) is 118.7 Hz. These scale
linearly with shaft speed and must be recomputed whenever the speed changes.
Note that BPFO at 151.3 Hz sits within 4 Hz of the third shaft harmonic at
147.5 Hz: any spectrum used to separate them needs a resolution finer than
about 2 Hz, which at 25.6 kHz means a transform of at least 16384 samples.

chunks.title: Envelope analysis
chunks.text:
Rolling-element defects are impacts, and impacts show far more clearly in the
envelope of the high-frequency band than in the raw velocity spectrum. Apply
envelope demodulation and look for a line at the defect frequency with
sidebands at shaft speed. An envelope peak at BPFO with shaft-speed sidebands
is the definitive indication of outer-race wear; the same peak without
sidebands more often indicates a lubrication problem than a spall.

chunks.title: Outer-race wear
chunks.text:
Elevated amplitude at BPFO in the envelope spectrum indicates outer-race wear
with high confidence. The overall velocity RMS rises as the defect develops,
crossing into zone C in the later stages, and the bearing temperature follows
with a lag of days to weeks. Causes are loss or degradation of lubricant,
contamination of the grease with water or process fluid, and a shaft or housing
seat outside the tolerances in section 4.3. The mitigation is bearing
replacement per section 4.2, preceded where contamination is suspected by the
flush in section 3.4.

chunks.title: Inner-race wear
chunks.text:
Elevated amplitude at BPFI indicates inner-race wear. The inner race rotates
with the shaft, so the defect passes in and out of the load zone once per
revolution and the envelope line carries strong sidebands spaced at shaft
speed. Inner-race defects usually follow a fitting fault or a shock load rather
than lubrication, and a machine that has been dropped or driven onto its
bearings is the usual history.

chunks.title: Misalignment
chunks.text:
Misalignment raises the second shaft harmonic, and the diagnostic quantity is
the ratio of 2X to 1X rather than the amplitude of either: a 2X-to-1X ratio
above 0.5 indicates misalignment, and above 1.0 indicates it strongly. A third
harmonic rises with it when the misalignment is angular. The overall velocity
level may stay inside zone A throughout, which is why a machine can be
significantly misaligned and still pass an absolute vibration check. A strong
axial component at 1X and 2X distinguishes angular from parallel misalignment.
Causes are a settled or soft foot, thermal growth of the motor not allowed for
in the cold alignment, pipe strain on the casing nozzles, and a coupling
element that has hardened. Mitigation is the alignment in section 4.4, after
the soft-foot check and after the coupling inspection in section 4.5.

chunks.title: Imbalance
chunks.text:
Imbalance raises the first shaft harmonic with little change at 2X, and the
response is radial and roughly equal in all radial directions. It is separated
from misalignment by the 2X-to-1X ratio staying low. Causes are product
build-up on the impeller, erosion of one vane, and a lost balance weight.
Mitigation is cleaning or in-situ balancing.

chunks.title: Cavitation
chunks.text:
Cavitation is a random process, not a periodic one: collapsing vapour bubbles
ring the casing and raise a broadband, spiky noise floor. The tell is
impulsiveness rather than loudness — kurtosis above 4.0 and crest factor above
5.0 — accompanied by an oscillation on the suction pressure at roughly 0.3 Hz
and a fall in suction pressure relative to the regime baseline. Most of the
energy sits above the 1000 Hz band that the ISO overall level measures, which
is why overall velocity RMS is a poor cavitation detector and why the
monitoring set carries kurtosis and crest alongside it. Causes are insufficient
NPSH available, a blocked or partly closed suction strainer, a suction lift
that has increased with falling tank level, and operation far below the best
efficiency point. Mitigation is to restore NPSH: check the strainer, raise the
suction level, and throttle the discharge to move the duty point back toward
best efficiency. Prolonged cavitation pits the impeller as in section 4.7.

chunks.title: Seal leakage
chunks.text:
A failing mechanical seal shows first on the process channels rather than on
vibration: delivered flow falls by ten to twenty per cent against the regime
baseline while discharge pressure falls more slowly, and motor current falls
with the load. Visible drip at the gland confirms it. Causes are face wear at
the end of seal life, dry running during a loss of suction, solids in the
pumped fluid scoring the faces, and a shaft sleeve worn by a previous seal.
Mitigation is the seal replacement in section 4.6. A leak that reaches the
drive-end bearing housing contaminates the grease and becomes a cause of the
outer-race wear in section 5.4.

chunks.title: Looseness
chunks.text:
Mechanical looseness produces a spectrum with many harmonics of shaft speed,
often with half-order components, and a directional response that is much
higher in one radial axis than the other. Distinguish it from misalignment by
checking that the alignment readings are within the tolerances in section 4.4
and by checking the hold-down torque in section 4.8.

chunks.title: Trending and baselines
chunks.text:
Judge every reading against the baseline for its own regime. A level that is
normal at high load can be a fifty per cent rise at low load, and a detector
that compares against a single machine-wide baseline will either miss the rise
or alarm on the regime change. Re-baseline after any work that changes the
machine's mechanical state, including bearing replacement and alignment.

chunks.title: Alarm response
chunks.text:
At a first warning, confirm the reading with a second measurement at the same
duty point before acting, then inspect within the shift. At a critical level,
plan a shutdown rather than continuing to run: the damage rate above zone C
rises sharply and a bearing that is caught in zone C is usually a bearing
change, while one caught in zone D often takes the shaft and the seal with it.

chunks.title: Start-up
chunks.text:
Prime the casing, open the suction valve fully, crack the discharge valve, and
start against a near-closed discharge. Open the discharge to duty within thirty
seconds: running against a closed discharge recirculates the whole flow and
heats the casing. Expect a vibration transient during run-up and do not judge
the machine's condition from it.

chunks.title: Minimum flow
chunks.text:
Do not run below 30 m³/h, which is twenty-five per cent of rated flow.
Operation below the minimum-flow line causes suction and discharge
recirculation, which produces a cavitation-like signature on the vibration
channels without any loss of NPSH, and damages the impeller in the same way.

chunks.title: NPSH
chunks.text:
The pump requires 3.2 m NPSH at rated flow and 4.6 m at 120 per cent of rated
flow. Available NPSH falls as the suction tank level falls, as the strainer
blocks, and as the fluid temperature rises toward its vapour pressure. Any of
the three can put the machine into cavitation without a change in the pump
itself.

chunks.title: Shutdown
chunks.text:
Close the discharge valve, stop the motor, then close the suction valve. Leave
the casing full unless the machine is being opened. Where the machine will be
idle for more than a month, turn the shaft by hand a quarter turn weekly to
avoid false brinelling of the stationary bearings.

chunks.title: What to record
chunks.text:
Record every intervention against the running-hour counter: regreasing,
alignment readings cold and hot, bearing changes with the bearings' markings,
seal changes, and the vibration and temperature baselines measured after the
work. A condition-monitoring system that is re-baselined without a record of
why cannot distinguish an improvement from a reset.
